n: In this topic we consider the forensic medical examination of living persons. Examinations of living persons are among those most often carried out in practice. They are ordered in criminal, civil and administrative cases. The largest number of examinations in the work of forensic medical institutions are connected with the infliction of bodily injuries. Examination of bodily injuries is carried out under the “Rules for the Forensic Medical Determination of the Severity of Bodily Injuries” in accordance with the Criminal Code. That is, first of all we deal with the question of the degree of severity of the injury.

t: Cases in which examination is ordered
n: Now we consider in which cases examination is ordered. Examination is ordered in five areas: injury, sexual condition, sexual crime, state of health and age. In bodily injuries the nature and degree of severity of the injury are determined. In sexual conditions sex, virginity, sexual maturity and pregnancy are considered, and in sexual crimes rape, sodomy and lewd acts. In the state of health, simulation, dissimulation, aggravation, artificial disease and self-mutilation are established. Examination is carried out in outpatient, district, city and inter-district departments and, if necessary, also in treatment institutions.

We consider which questions are resolved in the examination of bodily injuries. Examination is carried out in accordance with the Criminal Code and the rules for determining severity. First the type of injury and its location on the body are established. Then the instrument or means that inflicted the injury, the mechanism of formation and the time of infliction are determined. Finally the degree of severity is determined, with the qualifying feature indicated. Remember: all the information must be recorded in the “Expert's Opinion”.

Now the legal classification of bodily injuries. The Criminal Code divides injuries into grave, of moderate severity and light. Grave injury is given in Article 104: it involves danger to life, loss of function, termination of pregnancy, mental disorder or disfigurement. In grave injury 33% or more of working capacity is lost. In injury of moderate severity health is disturbed for more than 21 days, and working capacity is lost by 10-33%. Light injury is specified in Article 109 and is divided into two kinds: simple light, that is, health disturbance up to 6 days, and light injury with short-term health disturbance, that is, 6-21 days and up to 10%.

t: Difference between forensic medical and clinical assessment
n: The forensic medical degree of severity and the severity of the condition in the clinic are not the same concept. The same state of injury is assessed in two ways. The forensic medical assessment has its own criteria, whereas the clinical assessment is used for another purpose. The aims and criteria of the two assessments differ, so the results may not coincide. Note: a clinical “grave condition” does not mean a forensic medical “grave bodily injury”. These two terms must not be confused.

The first criterion is danger to life. Injuries that directly threaten life or give rise to a threatening state are regarded as dangerous to life. As examples one can name wounds penetrating a cavity, skull fracture, severe brain contusion and injury of a large artery. The chain is: the injury is inflicted, a threat to life arises, and this threat is connected with the injury. It is important that even if medical aid removes the threat, the injury is still assessed as dangerous to life. As a result the assessment is grave bodily injury.

t: Criterion: loss of general working capacity
n: The second criterion is loss of general working capacity. General working capacity is the ability to look after oneself and to perform work that does not require qualification. Remember: general capacity is not the same as professional capacity; in determining severity only general capacity is taken, whereas professional capacity is taken into account in civil cases. Temporary loss is expressed in days, and persistent loss in percentages. In grave injury the loss is 33 per cent or more, in moderate severity 10-33 per cent, and in light short-term injury up to 10 per cent. Disturbance beyond 120 days is conventionally regarded as persistent.

The third criterion is the duration of health disturbance. This is the criterion most often used in forensic medical practice. The period is determined in days on the basis of objective medical data. In light injury the disturbance is up to 6 days, in light short-term injury 6-21 days, and in moderate severity more than 21 days. Attention: the duration of treatment is not equal to the duration of disturbance. If treatment is prolonged because of late presentation, this prolongation is not taken into account.

To consolidate the criteria we consider four questions. First question: when health disturbance exceeds how many days is the injury of moderate severity? Answer: more than 21 days. Second question: at what proportion of persistent loss of general working capacity is the injury grave? Answer: 33% or more. Third question: to which degrees do a loss of up to 10% and of 10-33% correspond? Answer: light short-term and moderate severity, respectively. Fourth question: which criterion is expressed in per cent and which in days? Persistent loss is expressed in per cent, and the duration of disturbance in days.

Now the loss of sight, speech and hearing. Irreversible blindness in both eyes, or visual acuity of 0.04 and below, makes the injury grave. Loss of one healthy eye is also assessed as grave, because more than a third of working capacity is lost. If the tongue is lost entirely or by half, this too is grave injury. Complete deafness in both ears or inability to hear conversational speech at 3-5 cm from the ear is grave; with loss of hearing in one ear the injury is of moderate severity. Attention: if a non-seeing eye is lost, severity is determined by the duration of health disturbance.

t: Loss of an organ and of the ability to procreate
n: Now the loss of an organ and of the ability to procreate. Loss of an arm or leg means its separation or persistent loss of function, that is, paralysis. The hand and foot are equated with the arm and leg. In a man, procreation includes sexual intercourse and fertilisation. In a woman it includes intercourse, fertilisation, carrying the fetus and giving birth. If a state arises that prevents these functions, the ability to procreate is regarded as lost. An injury with loss of an organ or function, and also loss of one testis, ovary or kidney, is grave bodily injury.

t: Termination of pregnancy, mental disorder, disfigurement
n: We pass to the criteria of termination of pregnancy, mental disorder and disfigurement. The injury is assessed as grave only if there is a direct causal connection between the termination and the injury. Mental disorder is also regarded as grave bodily injury if directly causally connected with the injury. Indelible disfigurement does not disappear with time or treatment; surgery is needed to remove it. A specialist is involved for each criterion: for termination of pregnancy, an obstetrician-gynaecologist; for mental disorder, a forensic psychiatrist, neurologist and neurosurgeon; for disfigurement, a plastic surgeon and cosmetologist.

The rules for applying the criteria must be remembered. To determine the degree, one of the medical criteria is sufficient. If there are several criteria, assessment is made by the criterion corresponding to the more severe degree. If multiple injuries in one incident aggravate each other's course, a single degree is given for the whole, while those inflicted at different times are assessed separately. Only consequences causally connected with the new injury are taken into account. Age, disease or defects of medical aid, for example deterioration due to late presentation, are not taken into account. If it is not possible to establish the nature of the injury or the outcome is uncertain, the degree of severity is not determined.

t: Case analysis: assessing a bodily injury
n: Now a case analysis. First situation: in a victim, health disturbance lasted 10 days, and no other criterion was found. To which degree does the injury belong? It is more than six days but not more than 21 days, so it is a light bodily injury causing short-term health disturbance. Second question: will the assessment change if in the same person the vision of the only eye that was healthy before the injury is completely lost? Yes. Loss of one eye removes more than a third of working capacity, and this is grave injury. Remember: the more severe criterion is chosen.

t: Examination of the state of health: grounds for ordering
n: Now the examination of the state of health and the grounds for ordering it. Examination is ordered when a person fails to appear at the summons of the investigator or court because of illness. The ability of a suspect, accused and defendant to take part in investigative and court actions, and to be held in custody, is also determined. Examination is carried out when, during execution of a sentence, a convict complains of his health and refuses to work. It is also ordered in deferment of execution of a sentence: in illness, pregnancy and childbirth. Examination is also needed when conscripts and servicemen refuse service.

t: Establishing the state of health and simulation
n: On establishing the state of health and simulation. Examination is ordered in failure to appear at a summons because of illness and to determine the ability of a suspect or accused to take part in investigative and court actions. It is carried out by a commission with clinician-specialists: medical documents are studied, the person is examined comprehensively, and sometimes observed in hospital. Simulation is the presentation by a healthy person of a non-existent disease. By various means he imitates subjective and objective signs. The simulator's complaints do not correspond to objective signs; for example, with strong tea he provokes tachycardia and imitates heart disease.

Methods of simulation and its detection. To detect simulation the person is observed for some time: even an experienced simulator cannot fully reproduce the totality and dynamics of the signs of a disease. The simulator usually shows treatment as ineffective; it is not recommended to prescribe treatment until the diagnosis is established. If a gastric ulcer is imitated, blood is mixed into the faeces or ascorbic acid is used. In heart disease strong tea and coffee are used. In pulmonary tuberculosis the sputum and radiograph of a real patient are used, and in pulmonary haemorrhage gum blood is added to the sputum. Some examinations are carried out without warning, suddenly and repeatedly.

We compare aggravation and dissimulation. Aggravation is exaggeration of the signs of an existing disease or trauma; here mainly subjective signs are involved, and objective and subjective signs are compared. In simulation, by contrast, a non-existent disease is shown. Simulation and aggravation may be intentional, that is, purposeful, to escape punishment, or pathological, that is, purposeless. Dissimulation is deliberate concealment of a disease or injury; it is the opposite of simulation and is less frequent. Pilots, divers and drivers are examples.

Dissimulation: who conceals what. Dissimulation is the opposite of simulation; it is relatively rare and is always intentional, with the aim of concealing disease. The first group are cases where special requirements are set for health: entrants to military schools, pilots, divers, drivers of transport. The second group is concealment to escape responsibility: a driver guilty in a road traffic accident conceals intoxication, and a criminal conceals an existing injury. In some cases pregnancy, a past delivery or abortion is concealed.

Artificial diseases. Their aim is similar to simulation, but methods are used that do not create a serious threat to life. In internal organs such diseases are less frequent. In the skin and under it, binding a limb tightly or light blows produce swelling, and injection of paraffin or Vaseline under the skin forms a tumour. In internal organs, a lot of laxative or soap solution gives gastroenteritis, a lot of table salt nephrosonephritis, and ephedrine signs of hypertension. Dust or acid in the eye causes conjunctivitis and keratitis, and a foreign body is inserted into the ear. In artificial rectal prolapse there is injury at the anus.

On self-mutilation. Self-mutilation is purposeful, deliberate infliction of injury on oneself, for example to evade military service. The injury is often on the hand, especially in the region of the palm; it is inflicted with a sharp or firearm weapon, usually by the person himself. The signs are as follows: the injury is in a region within reach of the hand, more often on the left; nearby there are several superficial wounds; in amputation the fingers are cut at different levels; with a firearm the shot is usually fired in contact or from close range. In an investigative experiment, the situation described by the person is checked under conditions close to the incident.

A case analysis on simulation and self-mutilation. First situation: a conscript, using nothing, shows reduced hearing. His complaint does not correspond to the results of objective examination. Is it simulation or dissimulation? In simulation a non-existent disease is shown, and in dissimulation an existing disease is concealed. Second situation: on the palm, next to the main injury, there are several superficial incised wounds, and the fingers are amputated at different levels. What does this indicate? Attention: simulation is not aggravation. In simulation there is no disease, and in aggravation the signs of an existing disease or trauma are shown as more severe.

Examination to determine sex. In issuing documents, marriage, alimony and sexual crime cases, where there is doubt about sex, examination is necessary. Hermaphroditism is the presence in one person of organs characteristic of both sexes; in practice the pseudo form is more frequent. In true hermaphroditism there are male and female glands. In the pseudo male type there is a scrotum and spermatogenesis is observed, with external features resembling the female. In the pseudo female type there is an ovary and oogenesis is observed, with external features resembling the male. In the examination, history, medical documents, anthropometry and laboratory are used; leucocyte chromosomes show the genetic sex.

Determining sexual maturity. Sexual maturity is the degree of development that makes it possible to lead a sexual life without harm to health; in girls it means intercourse, pregnancy, childbirth and nursing. Up to 14 years a person is regarded as immature. In the Criminal Code liability is tied to age: in Articles 118-119, 18 and 14; in Articles 128-129, 16 years. The norm: height standing at least 150 cm, sitting 80 cm, chest circumference 78-80 cm; pelvic dimensions 26-27, 29 cm and external conjugate 17-18 cm. These indices are relative: childbirth is possible even with smaller dimensions, and with acceleration they may be larger. The examination is carried out with the participation of an obstetrician-gynaecologist.

Determining virginity. Virginity is determined by the anatomical integrity of the hymen; the forms of the hymen fall into 3 groups. Defloration usually occurs at first intercourse, but may also result from a finger, an object or an operation. Attention: a tear is not a natural notch. A tear is most often on the clock face between 5 and 7, whereas a notch usually does not reach the base. Healing of a tear proceeds in stages: at first bleeding, swelling and blood clots; later the swelling decreases and a whitish coating appears; by the end of the 1st week granulation tissue begins to cover it; in the 2nd-3rd week a scar forms and the inflammation subsides.

Quick questions on virginity and maturity. First question: up to what time can the period of violation of the integrity of the hymen be determined? In the first weeks; after three weeks this question cannot be resolved. Second question: if there is suspicion about virginity, whom should one consult within a short time? Forensic medical experts, not obstetrician-gynaecologists. Third question: for how many days does semen persist in the vagina? Usually 3-5 days; the sooner the sample is taken, the more reliable the result. Fourth question: what are the edges of an old tear like? Relatively thick and scarred.

Determining the ability to procreate. In a man, procreation is sexual intercourse and fertilisation; in a woman, the possibility of sexual intercourse, becoming pregnant and giving birth. Impotence is associated with diseases of the central nervous system and endocrine system and with defects of the external genital organ; functional impotence from a neurotic reaction also occurs. The ability to fertilise is assessed by laboratory examination of the ejaculate. If azoospermia, necrospermia or asthenozoospermia is found, this ability is denied. In a woman, age prevents pregnancy, that is, the period before puberty and the menopause. Diseases and defects of the genital organs, tumours, and removal of the uterus, tube or ovary also prevent it.

Determining pregnancy and past delivery. In an ongoing pregnancy menstruation stops, the mammary glands enlarge, and the areola darkens from the 2nd month. The size, shape and density of the uterus change. In the laboratory the pregnancy hormone, chorionic gonadotropin, is determined. In the second half whitish streaks appear on the abdomen and pigmentation along the midline. Reliable signs: the fetal heartbeat on auscultation, and fetal parts and movements on palpation and ultrasound. The duration is determined as in obstetrics. After delivery, at first the mammary glands are swollen and the cervix is open. In a woman who has given birth the external os is slit-like, and in one who has not it is usually round. A considerable time after delivery one can say only that delivery has occurred.

Determining abortion. Abortion is termination of pregnancy before 22 weeks. It may be spontaneous or artificial. Medical abortion is performed by an obstetrician-gynaecologist in a medical institution; up to 12 weeks on request, later on indication, observing the rules, with examination and follow-up. Criminal abortion is performed by an untrained worker or an ordinary person and entails criminal liability under Article 114 of the Criminal Code. The traces correspond to the method: in mechanical, abrasions and bruises; in chemical, a chemical burn; in thermal, a thermal burn. Complications of criminal abortion: air embolism, traumatic shock, acute bleeding, perforation and poisoning.

A case analysis on sexual conditions. First situation: criminal abortion is suspected in a woman. On examination, abrasions, bruises and haemorrhages into the mucosa were found in the vagina and uterus. Which method may have been used? The mechanical method. In the chemical method, signs of a chemical burn and poisoning would be expected. Second situation: much time has passed since delivery; the external os of the cervix is slit-like, in place of the hymen there are myrtle-like papillae, and there are scars on the abdominal skin. What can the expert record? Only that delivery has occurred. In a later period the possibility of deciding the exact time is limited.

Rape. Article 118: sexual intercourse against the will by violence, threat or taking advantage of helplessness. In violence, bruises and abrasions are found, especially on the inner surface of the thighs and the genital organs, as well as a tear of the hymen and traces of semen. Attention: a threat leaves no trace, and injury to the vagina may occur even in women who lead a sexual life. Stages of examination: first the ruling and the record are studied, then the interview and gynaecological history are collected. Then, on examination, injuries and helplessness are checked. For traces of semen, a smear and an imprint are taken quickly, and finally laboratory examination is carried out.

On sodomy. Article 120: satisfaction by a man of sexual need with a man without violence. Both the active and the passive participant are liable. On the active participant, on the penis and in the pubic region, blood, hair, particles of faeces and an oily substance belonging to the second man may be found; in the coronal sulcus these persist for a long time. In the passive participant, abrasions, haemorrhages and fissures are found at the anus and in the rectum. In regular intercourse the sphincter weakens and the folds become smooth. Attention: signs of constipation, proctitis and haemorrhoids may be wrongly interpreted. If there was violence, only the active person is liable under Article 119.

t: Lewd acts, venereal diseases and HIV
n: Lewd acts, venereal diseases and HIV. Article 129: sexual indecent-lewd acts against a person under 16. In this there may be no traces of injury; redness, abrasions and bruises are found as signs. Article 113: knowingly infecting with a venereal disease or HIV, that is, human immunodeficiency virus, is a crime. Article 129 belongs to the group of crimes against the family, youth and morality, and Article 113 to the crimes dangerous to life or health. In this case the disease and the source of infection are established. The examination is carried out with the participation of a dermatovenereologist and an HIV specialist; a person at a late stage becomes a subject of the crime.

A case analysis on sexual crimes. Situation: a woman is brought for examination on suspicion of rape. The expert has been provided with the ruling of appointment, the record of the scene inspection and medical documents. The expert first familiarises himself with these materials, then asks the woman about the details of the incident and collects the gynaecological history, that is, information on menstruation, the last intercourse and pregnancy. Attention: Article 118 is rape, and Article 119 is satisfaction of sexual need in a perverted manner. Do not confuse them. Think: why are a smear from inside the vagina and imprints from the external regions taken as soon as possible after the incident? Should the suspect also be examined?

t: General algorithm of conducting the examination
n: The general algorithm of conducting the examination. The basis: the Criminal and Civil Codes, the procedural codes, the law “On Forensic Examination” and the Instruction. The procedure and methodology are determined by the features of the incident and the tasks set before the examination. The algorithm consists of six stages. In the first stage the circumstances of the incident are studied first of all from the information in the ruling or order appointing the examination. In the second, the original medical documents are studied. The third is interview of the person and complaints, the fourth is inspection with instruments. The fifth stage is laboratory examination and consultation, and the last is the expert's opinion.

The procedure for documents, identification, interview and inspection. In the interview it is clarified when, where, by whom, with what and how many times harm was inflicted. Inspection is carried out with instruments, that is, a ruler and a magnifying glass; the injury is photographed only with the person's permission. The medical document must be in the original, and the person who ordered the examination is responsible for its authenticity. For identification a passport, military ID or certificate is needed. In sexual conditions, besides the document, 2 photographs are required. A minor is examined in the presence of parents or a teacher. The person who ordered may be present; when a person of the other sex is undressed, the investigator leaves the room.

t: Quick question: rules of presence at inspection
n: The rules of presence at inspection. The person who ordered the examination may be present at the inspection. Only if an undressed person of the other sex is examined does the investigator leave the examination room. Examination of minors is carried out in the presence of parents or teachers, and of legally incapable persons in the presence of a legal representative. Examination of a patient under treatment, if his health permits, takes place in the presence of the person who ordered it or his representative and the treating physician; this is recorded in the medical history. Question: who must be present when a minor child is brought for examination, and why? Think through the answer yourself.

A case analysis on the order of examination. Situation: an investigator ordered an examination on the injury of a minor girl. Her parents accompany her, and only a copy of the medical document has been brought. Question: in what sequence does the expert work, and is a copy of the document alone sufficient? The expert's sequence: circumstances of the incident, medical documents, interview of the person, inspection, additional examination or consultation if necessary, then the expert's opinion. Attention: risk of error! Originals of medical documents are required. The person who ordered the examination is responsible for authenticity.

Conclusion of the topic. A bodily injury is grave, of moderate severity or light. The criteria: danger to life, duration of disturbance, that is, 6 and 21 days, and loss of working capacity, that is, 10% and 33%. One criterion is sufficient; if there are several, the more severe is applied. Individual characteristics and defects of medical aid are not taken into account in determining severity. Simulation is presenting a non-existent disease, aggravation is exaggerating an existing one, and dissimulation is concealment; these are examined by a commission. For the paediatrician: to write the medical document objectively and fully, to send the child for examination together with the parents, and, when virginity is in question, to refer to a forensic medical expert more quickly.
